name_en: Jun Shan Yin Zhen (Junshan Silver Needle)
cultivar: Junshan local landrace and Fuding Dabai
processing: Buds only: pan-fired, lightly dried, then wrapped in paper or cloth in small bundles to 'sweat' (men huang) for a day or more, dried again, re-wrapped for a second yellowing, and finished with a slow low-temperature drying; the whole cycle takes about three days.
harvest_season: A short window around Qingming in early April, buds only; nothing else of the year is sold under the name.
appearance_dry: Fat, straight single buds in golden yellow with silvery down, 'gold wrapped in jade'.
appearance_wet: Plump pale-yellow buds that stand upright in a glass, sinking and rising a few times before settling.
taste_profile: Soft and sweet with sweet corn, fresh chestnut and a hint of honey, a mellow umami body and none of the grassy edge of a green bud tea.

brewing.notes: Tall glass at 80 °C, water first, then buds; wait and watch them stand, sink and rise. A gaiwan at 85 °C with slightly longer steeps gets more flavour but loses the show.

vintage_note: Sold only as the current year's spring harvest, picked in a short window around Qingming; it is one of the most expensive teas in China per gram because the island's output is tiny. Most 'Junshan Yinzhen' on the market is bud tea from the wider Yueyang area, and much of it is barely yellowed, closer to a green. Drink within the year, kept cold and sealed.
description:
Jun Shan Yin Zhen is the most famous yellow tea and almost the only one most people have heard of, a bud-only tea from Junshan, a small island in Dongting Lake near Yueyang in Hunan. The island is small and so is its output, so the genuine article is scarce by nature, and the tea has had a reputation for exclusivity since it was sent as a tribute tea in the Qing dynasty.

What makes it yellow is the sweating. After a light pan-firing and partial drying, the buds are wrapped in paper in small bundles and left in a warm room for a day or more, during which gentle heat and moisture let the chlorophyll break down and the harsh green compounds soften; then they are dried a little, wrapped again, and finally dried slowly. The whole cycle takes about three days, and the result is a bud that is golden rather than green, with a mellow sweetness in place of grassiness.

In the cup it is soft, sweet and gentle: sweet corn, fresh chestnut, a little honey, a rounded savoury body and no bite. It is a quiet tea, and its other pleasure is visual, which is why it is traditionally brewed in a tall glass: the buds stand on end, sink, rise and sink again as they take on water. Use 80 °C water, pour it first, and give it a full minute; it is not a tea for strong brewing.

Buying it is the hard part. The island's production is tiny and the price per gram is among the highest in China, so almost everything sold as Junshan Yinzhen is bud tea from the surrounding Yueyang hills (Beigang Mao Jian country), and a great deal of it skips or shortens the sweating and is really a green bud tea with a yellow name. A genuine lot is noticeably golden, not green, and tastes mellow, not grassy. If it is cheap, it is not from the island; if it is green, it is not yellow tea.

For a sense of what proper yellowing does without the price, Huo Shan Huang Ya from Anhui is the practical alternative.
history:
Tea from Junshan Island in Dongting Lake has a long pedigree on paper. Under the name Yonghu tea it is said to have been a tribute in the Tang, and in the Qing the island's tea was split into 'pointed' and 'fuzzy' kinds, with the pointed one sent to court as gong jian, 'tribute tips'. The older tea was not necessarily yellow in today's sense, and one account has the island making green tea before yellow took over.

The usual story of its origin is a legend: a kind young man named Zhang Shun received a shining pearl from the Dragon King and buried it on Qingluo Peak for the good of his village, and needle-shaped bushes grew on the spot. It is also often said to have been Mao Zedong's favourite tea, a claim that is widely repeated and hard to confirm.

The craft is better documented than the legends. Two rounds of wrapping in paper and resting in a box turn the buds gold, and picking rules are strict, the famous 'nine do-not-picks' for rain, frost, opened or hollow buds and so on. The method entered China's national intangible heritage list in 2021 and was part of the 2022 UNESCO inscription of Chinese tea traditions, the only yellow tea named. Output is very small, about 1,000 kg a year by one estimate, and a green-style version also circulates under the name.
